title: Intrauterine insemination (IUI) | NHS inform
text:
Intrauterine insemination (IUI)
Not all information on this page will be relevant for everyone. All couples can access NHS fertility services if they meet the
treatment access criteria
. This includes same-sex couples and couples where one or both partners are trans or non-binary.
Intrauterine insemination (IUI) is a fertility treatment. It helps people with
infertility
issues try to conceive. The procedure involves placing sperm directly into the womb (uterus).
Who needs IUI?
IUI is suitable for a variety of people, including non-binary or transgender people. It is often recommended for:
Donor sperm
When necessary, donor sperm may be used to help get pregnant. This can be for various reasons, like for same-sex couples or when a male partner has low quality sperm.
Cervical issues
If the cervical mucus is too thick, it can block sperm from reaching the egg. IUI goes through the cervix, putting sperm directly into the womb.
Ovulation issues
Conditions like
polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)
or irregular ovulation may require IUI.
Ejaculation issues
Some people may have difficulty ejaculating. This includes retrograde ejaculation (when sperm goes into the bladder rather than out of the penis).
What can affect IUI success?
Several factors can influence the success of IUI, including:
age – success rates decrease as you get older
sperm quality – higher sperm count, and motility (ability to move) increase chances of successful fertilisation
the health of the fallopian tube – for IUI, you need at least 1 open fallopian tube (the tube that connects ovaries to uterus) for sperm to reach the egg
uterine health – uterine abnormalities, fibroids, or scar tissue can affect implantation (when a fertilized egg attaches to the lining of the uterus)
timing – success rates improve when IUI is done when during ovulation
previous pregnancies – previous successful pregnancies can mean improved outcomes
Smoking tobacco, drinking too much alcohol, obesity, and high stress can negatively impact fertility.
Getting Started with IUI
The process typically involves several steps.
Consultation
A fertility specialist will evaluate your health. They’ll discuss the best options for you and explain the IUI process.
Checking your fallopian tubes
The fallopian tubes may be checked to ensure that they are healthy and open. This is so an egg can travel from the ovary to the womb. This will be done using ultrasound or an x-ray.
Ovarian stimulation
You may have IUI during the time in your normal menstrual cycle where you produce eggs. Alternatively, you may be given drugs to stimulate your ovaries to produce eggs.
Monitoring
You may have a scan or blood tests to monitor the growth of your eggs. You may also be given a hormone to help release an egg from your ovary (ovulation).
Insemination
On the day of insemination, the sperm will be inserted into your womb through the cervix. This is done using a fine catheter (tube).
Pregnancy Test
About 10 to 14 days after the embryo transfer a pregnancy test will be performed. A scan will be repeated a few weeks later to confirm pregnancy.
If you become pregnant you will be discharged for maternity care.
If you are unsuccessful, you may be invited for a review appointment. Your fertility specialist may advise repeating IUI or may discuss further possible treatment options.
